newsitem.title: USA: US sees bigger role in Caspian energy development.
newsitem.headline: US sees bigger role in Caspian energy development.

text.p: The U.S. government needs to increase its support for U.S. energy companies to develop oil and natural gas resources in the Caspian Basin, according to a State Department report.

"Other governments have recognized the commercial opportunities in the region and have come in strongly in support of their companies with high-level engagement, extensive credit lines and other incentives," said the report prepared for the Senate Appropriations Committee.

The U.S. government "needs to enhance its efforts throughout the region to support American companies in similar fashion and continue to bring U.S. companies to this market," the State Department report said.
The Caspian region has oil reserves estimated from 90 billion barrels, which would be comparable to Iran, up to 200 billion, which would put it second to the entire Middle East, the report said.

Earlier oil industry estimates had put proven reserves at 27.5 billion barrels with an additional 40 to 60 billion barrels of estimated reserves divided unequally between Caspian bordering countries of Iran, Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkemenistan and Azerbaijan.
The region's natural gas reserves are estimated at 7.9 trillion cubic meters, putting it third behind the Middle East and Russia, it said.

With such high stakes, the report recommended more high-level government interaction with the region through trade missions and export credits, and visits of congressmen, administration and business officials.
For example, it suggested cabinet-level participation in oil and gas shows in the region, as well as invitations to region's leaders to visit the United States.
It also urged using programs from the Overseas Private Investment Corp, the Trade Development Agency and the U.S. Export-Import Bank to nurture a relationship with the region.

The report reaffirmed the Clinton administration's opposition to a 1992 measure that barred U.S. assistance to Azerbaijan, which has 3.6 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, until the Azerbaijan government takes steps to stop blockades and other uses of force against Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh.

That measure hinders U.S. policy objectives such as providing humanitarian aid and supporting democratic and economic development, the report said, and disadvantages U.S. firms by limiting the government's ability to provide financial support such as risk insurance and grants for pipeline studies.
The report also called for the United States to support a United Nations-led peace process in Afghanistan when, or if, terms to end the conflict there are reached.
It also said the United States should push for improved navigation systems in the Bosporus, the key strait for oil shipping.

To try to develop alternative routes to the Bosporus, the report called for encouraging market development in the Black Sea region to develop the infrastructure to transport Caspian energy to other markets.
